definitions.explanation: Describes an act or a person carrying great moral, religious, or emotional guilt. While it can literally describe sins in a religious sense, in everyday Japanese it is often used exaggeratedly (sometimes playfully) to mean "deeply wrong" or "too irresistibly tempting" — as when a dessert is so good it feels sinful to eat.

examples.japanese: {罪深|つみぶか}い{行|おこな}い。
{夜中|よなか}にケーキを{食|た}べるなんて、なんて{罪深|つみぶか}いんだろう。
examples.english: Eating cake in the middle of the night — how sinful of me.

examples.japanese: {彼|かれ}は{自分|じぶん}のしたことがどれほど{罪深|つみぶか}いかを{理解|りかい}し、{深|ふか}く{後悔|こうかい}していた。
examples.english: He understood how deeply wrong what he had done was, and was deeply remorseful.

notes:
Composed of {罪|つみ} (sin, crime, guilt) and the suffix -{深|ぶか}い (deep). The compound literally means "having deep sin." It ranges from literal religious or legal "sinful" to metaphorical use in everyday speech, where it frequently appears as an exaggerated, half-joking description of irresistible indulgences.

USAGE:
- Serious use: describes acts that violate moral or religious principles
- Light/playful use: describes guilty pleasures (rich food, sleeping in, skipping work)
- Self-deprecating use: speakers use it about their own indulgences with a wry tone

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {罪深|つみぶか}い{行|おこな}い: a sinful act
- {罪深|つみぶか}い{人間|にんげん}: a sinful person
- なんて{罪深|つみぶか}いんだろう: how sinful (of me/them)!
- {罪深|つみぶか}い{味|あじ}: a sinfully good taste (informal, of food)

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {罪|つみ}な: cruel, heartless — often of someone toying with others' feelings
- {悪|わる}い: bad — general-purpose, much weaker
- {邪悪|じゃあく}な: evil, wicked — stronger, more formal
- {後|あと}ろめたい: guilty-feeling — emphasizes the internal feeling of guilt

forms.label: Conditional たら
forms.negative: {罪深|つみぶか}くなかったら
